info.title: Bowler
info.description:
Bowler delivers webhooks for a company that wants to send events to its own customers' servers. It signs each one following the Standard Webhooks specification, retries failures on a schedule, never lets one slow receiver hold up the others, and keeps the history of every attempt.

**Vocabulary.** An *app* is one of your own customers. An *endpoint* is a URL that app wants events sent to. A *message* is one event. A *delivery* is one message going to one endpoint, and an *attempt* is one try at a delivery.

**Delivery guarantee.** At least once. A crash or a retry can cause the same message to arrive twice, so a receiver should ignore a `webhook-id` it has already seen. A message is never lost once the API has answered `202`.

**Retention.** Finished messages, with their deliveries and attempts, are deleted after the operator's retention period, 30 days by default. A message that still has work to do is never deleted.

**Credentials.** The operator's API key can do everything. An app's own side can be given a *token* instead, made with `POST /v1/apps/{app}/tokens`: it works on that app only, and another app looks the same as one that does not exist. A token can be made read only, and can be made to expire. The routes that make apps and tokens, and the metrics, take the operator's key only.

**Audit log.** Changes to endpoints and tokens, and every read or rotation of a signing secret, are recorded with who did them. See `GET /v1/apps/{app}/audit-log`.

**Signing secrets at rest.** If the operator sets an encryption key, signing secrets are stored encrypted. This does not change the API.

parameters.name: Idempotency-Key
parameters.description: Send the same key again and you get the original message back, marked with `Idempotent-Replayed: true`, instead of a second send. Use it so that retrying a request whose answer you never received is safe. A key is remembered as long as its message is kept, which is the retention period (30 days unless the operator changed it). After that the same key is accepted as a new message.

post.description: The message is stored and one delivery is created for every endpoint that wants this event type, in one step. The answer is `202`, because delivery happens afterwards.

post.description: Bowler sends this request to an endpoint's URL. The body is the message payload exactly as you sent it. Verify the signature before trusting it: the `signature` Go package does it in one call, and any Standard Webhooks library works too. Answer with a `2xx` to accept. Anything else is retried. `410 Gone` switches the endpoint off. Redirects are not followed.

parameters.name: webhook-id
parameters.description: The message id. The same on every attempt, so a receiver can recognize a repeat and ignore it.

parameters.name: webhook-timestamp
parameters.description: Seconds since the Unix epoch, when this attempt was made. Reject one that is too far from your clock to stop replays.

parameters.name: webhook-signature
parameters.description: One or more space separated signatures, each `v1,` followed by the base64 HMAC-SHA256 of `<webhook-id>.<webhook-timestamp>.<body>`. Two appear while a secret is being rotated.

apiKey.description: The key set in `BOWLER_API_KEY`. Anyone who has it can read and change everything, including the tokens of every app.

appToken.description: A token made for one app with `POST /v1/apps/{app}/tokens`. It starts with `bwl_` and works on that app's routes only: its endpoints, messages, deliveries and audit log. It cannot make apps or tokens, read metrics or see another app, and another app looks the same as one that does not exist. A token made with `"scope": "read"` may look and change nothing, and cannot read a signing secret. A token made with `expires_in_hours` stops working after that time. Safe to give to that app's own side, such as a settings page for its customers.

app.name: app
app.description: An app id, or the `uid` you gave it.

request_id.description: Quote this when asking for help. It is also in the `X-Request-ID` header.

DeliveryState.description: `pending` is waiting for its time. `inflight` is being tried. `failed` can be replayed. `cancelled` means its endpoint was deleted.

Failure.description: Why an attempt did not succeed, in terms you can act on.

response_snippet.description: The start of the receiver's reply, cut short.

prefix.description: The first characters of the token, to tell tokens apart. Not enough to use it.

revoked_at.description: Present once the token has been revoked.

scope.description: `full` can do everything its app may. `read` can look and change nothing, and cannot read a signing secret.

expires_at.description: When the token stops working. Absent for a token that does not expire.

last_used_at.description: Roughly when the token was last used, to within ten minutes. Absent if it never was.

token.description: The token itself. Shown once, here, and never again: only a hash is kept. Store it now.

actor_id.description: `admin` for the operator's key, or the id of the token.

action.description: One of: app.create, token.create, token.revoke, endpoint.create, endpoint.update, endpoint.delete, endpoint.secret_read, endpoint.secret_rotate, endpoint.recover, delivery.replay.

detail.description: A little about what happened. For an update, the names of the fields changed, never their values. Never a secret, token or payload.

request_id.description: The `X-Request-ID` of the request, to connect an entry to the server log.
